posts.title: Writing a brief that finds the right person
posts.excerpt: What to put in a vacancy brief, and what to leave out.
posts.content:
Most hiring problems start with a brief that describes a job title instead of a job. "Warehouse operative" or "receptionist" tells a candidate very little. What do they do on a Tuesday afternoon, and who do they do it with?

Start with the week, not the list

Write down what a normal week looks like: the shifts, the busy periods, the tasks that take longest and the ones nobody likes. Candidates can imagine themselves in that, and the ones who cannot will say so early, which saves everybody time.

Be honest about the awkward parts. If the loading bay is cold in January or the front desk is hectic at nine, say so. People who accept a job knowing this tend to stay.

Say who they will work with

The team matters as much as the task. Tell us who the new person reports to, how big the team is and how the manager likes to work. That is why we visit the site and meet the people involved before we start looking.

Keep the must-haves short

A long list of requirements shuts out good people. Pick the few things that cannot be learned in a month, and treat everything else as a bonus. We will help you decide which is which.

posts.title: What to expect from a first interview
posts.excerpt: A calm guide to the first conversation with an employer.
posts.content:
A first interview is mostly a conversation between two people who are both trying to decide whether this will work. It helps to remember that you are deciding too.

Before you go

Find out where the building is and how long the journey takes at that time of day. Read the job description again and think of one or two examples from past work that match it. Your consultant will tell you what we know about the manager and the team, so ask us.

In the room

You will usually be asked about your experience, what you enjoy and what a good day looks like. Answer plainly. If you do not know something, say so and say how you would find out. Employers tend to remember honesty far longer than a polished answer.

Your questions

Ask about the hours, the team, what the first month will involve and how people are supported at the start. Those answers tell you more than the job description does.

Afterwards

Ring your consultant the same day if you can. Tell us how it felt, whatever you thought. We will pass on what is useful and help with what comes next, including a no.

posts.title: Agency workers and holiday pay, explained
posts.excerpt: How an hourly rate, holiday pay and an agency margin fit together.
posts.content:
When an employer takes on an agency worker, the invoice can look confusing. Here is how ours works, in plain words.

What the worker receives

The worker is paid for every hour they work, and they build up holiday pay as they go. They never pay us anything.

What the employer is billed

The employer is billed by the hour at the worker's pay rate, plus a margin of 26%. That margin covers the worker's holiday pay, employer costs such as National Insurance and the pension contribution, and our own time finding, checking and supporting them.

Why it is set out like this

We would rather you saw how the number is made than guessed at it. If the worker's rate changes, the bill changes with it, and nothing is added on the side. Timesheets are agreed with the supervisor each week, so there are no surprises at the end of the month.

If you are thinking of taking a temp on permanently, see our note on temp-to-perm. After 12 weeks there is no transfer fee.

posts.title: Why the first morning matters
posts.excerpt: A small thing that makes a big difference to who stays.
posts.content:
Many people decide within a day whether a new job is going to work. The first morning is when most of the nerves are, so it is worth getting right.

Someone at the door

We meet every new hire at the door on their first morning, introduce them to their manager and walk them in. A familiar face takes the edge off the unknown car park, the unfamiliar entrance and the question of where to put your coat.

What employers can do

Have a name badge or locker ready. Make sure the new person knows who to ask when we are not there. Plan a short first task they can finish, rather than leaving them to shadow someone all day. Tell the team they are coming.

After the first morning

We call both of you in week one, and visit at day 30. That is not a test. It is a chance to hear what is going well, to fix small problems before they grow and to record what you would want for the next hire.

A good start is rarely complicated. It mostly takes a little planning and a person who turns up on time.

posts.title: Temp-to-perm: when trying it first makes sense
posts.excerpt: Taking someone on after a temporary start, and why it can suit both sides.
posts.content:
Sometimes the best way to find out whether a job suits a person is to let them do it. Temp-to-perm lets an employer and a worker find out together.

How it works

The worker starts as an agency worker, billed by the hour at their pay rate plus our margin. If it goes well, the employer can take them on permanently. After 12 weeks there is no transfer fee at all.

When it suits

It tends to work well when a role is new and not fully defined, when the work is seasonal and might become year-round, or when a manager is unsure how a candidate will fit with the team. It also suits people who want to see the workplace before they commit to it.

What to watch for

Be clear from the start that the arrangement might become permanent, and say what you will look at. Talk to the worker honestly midway. We visit during the placement, so we can help both sides to have that conversation.

If either side decides it is not right, that is a perfectly good result. It is better to learn it in the first weeks than the first year.

posts.title: Keeping your CV short, true and current
posts.excerpt: Practical tips for a CV that is easy to read and easy to trust.
posts.content:
A CV does not need to be clever. It needs to be clear, accurate and easy to read in a couple of minutes by someone who is busy.

Lead with what you have done

Put your most recent job first, with your title, the name of the employer and the dates. Under it, write a few lines on what you actually did: the equipment you used, the people you worked with, the tasks you were trusted with.

Be straightforward about gaps

Time out for caring, health, study or moving house is normal. A single honest line is plenty. You do not owe anyone a long explanation, and we will help you decide how to say it.

Check the details

Make sure your phone number and email are right, and that the dates add up. Employers notice small errors, and they also notice when a CV is simply tidy.

Do not worry if you do not have one

If you have never written a CV, come and see us. We will sit down with you, ask about your work and write one together. It costs nothing, because job seekers never pay us anything.
